https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: The XR founder who wants to bring Britain to a standstill
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
When Roger Hallam and I meet, the first thing he does is hand me a piece of paper telling me I’m liable to go to prison in the next 20 years or so. And all I’d done was ask if he wanted a coffee. We are sitting in the corner of a starkly lit community café in Westminster. Steve Winwood’s Valerie plays over the stereo as Hallam speaks. “This is a little experiment with the truth, Tom. Hopefully you’ll be able to cope,” he says with a sportive laugh, before clearing his throat and reading out the contents of the document, which states that in a rapidly warming world journalists are likely to be prosecuted at the “climate Nuremberg trials’’ of the future. There is a dotted line at the bottom followed by a declaration to tell the truth about carbon emissions and, more pertinently, about those involved in protesting about them. “If you decide not to sign this agreement, or if you break it, you may be subject to nonviolent direct action and will be liable for prosecution at a later date for complicity in genocide.” He slides a pen across the table.
In fairness, I wasn’t expecting an exchange of pleasantries. The 56-year-old is not known for taking the softly-softly approach. As co-founder of the climate action groups Extinction Rebellion and Insulate Britain, he is the architect of arguably the most disruptive and radical protest movements this country has seen. At the height of its powers, Extinction Rebellion, known as XR, was able to lock down the centre of London for weeks at a time, with up to 10,000 people camping out on the capital’s bridges and major thoroughfares. Insulate Britain, considered a denomination of XR, barricaded motorways with human roadblocks. Just Stop Oil, the newest and most agile of the trio — which Hallam is involved with but didn’t set up — has blockaded oil terminals and thrown a tin of soup over Van Gogh’s Sunflowers. This weekend the three groups are hoping to enact the biggest act of protest yet, called The Big One, with a goal of mobilising 100,000 people across four days in London.
Sliding the pen back across the table, I reply that I’m confident enough in my powers of truth-telling for his contract not to be necessary, and we agree to move on. Over the course of our three hours together he will make clear at regular intervals his deep distrust of the media, which he sees as having consistently sought to hamstring his activities in forcing governments to decarbonise. For the most part, this amounts to the reporting of things that he has said. Shortly after Hallam described the Holocaust as “just another f***ery in human history” to a German newspaper in November 2019, XR announced that he would no longer be a part of the group’s strategic decision-making. A year later, he was again condemned when a recording emerged in which he said that MPs and business leaders would end up with bullets in their heads for their role in the degradation of the environment. Hallam contends that both of these quotes were taken out of context.
When we meet, he is wearing yet further evidence of his treatment by the press in the form of a gruel-grey prison-issue sweatshirt. One evening last November, his flat in Elephant and Castle in south London, which he shares with his 24-year-old partner, Frieda Luerken, a fellow activist, was raided by police after a Sun reporter listened in on a Zoom call in which he allegedly laid plans to block the M25. He was arrested, charged with conspiracy to commit a public nuisance and jailed on remand for more than three months at HMP Wandsworth, where he says he bunked with a spice (synthetic marijuana) addict who hotboxed their cell three times a day. “I don’t have many other jumpers,” he explains. Considering the scuff marks on his coat and the faint air of fustiness in our corner of the room, I am not inclined to doubt him.
Early on, he informs me that he won’t be answering all my questions. Which is true insomuch as he will respond to many of my inquiries with long and winding responses, which veer between sociological theory (“If you do something like Extinction Rebellion or Insulate Britain, it has a massive, broad, extensive causality in the social field”) and cataclysmic pronouncement (“My general rule of thumb is that since around 2005, the climate has been f***ed in this country as far as farming is concerned”). This is, I suspect, a learnt behaviour rather than one that comes naturally, a tactic to avoid producing the sort of quotable tags that have tripped him up in the past. (In fact, the only question he outright refuses to answer is why he so often reverts to analogies with Nazism and the Holocaust.)
Throughout our conversation he will repeatedly portray himself as an academic rather than an activist, and when challenged about his methods will fall back on “the literature”. But there is much that is unaffected and even, at times, strangely jovial about him too. Amid the talk of mass starvation, societal collapse and my future incarceration, he will on more than one occasion catch me by surprise when, at some small quip or another, he will laugh like a boy with a high and sudden guffaw.
I have been mildly fascinated by Hallam since 2018, when seemingly from nowhere XR emerged fully formed, and the following year went on to blockade London not once but twice through a series of occupations that led to the arrest of more than 3,000 people and a policing bill of £50 million. Hallam did not found XR alone. It was created by a small group of activists, academics and friends including Gail Bradbrook, a long-term environmental campaigner and the daughter of a West Yorkshire coal miner. But it was he who — after surfacing from the libraries of King’s College London (KCL), where he’d been studying civil disobedience in the day and sleeping beneath the desks at night — designed XR’s strategy, the central thesis of which posited that if enough people take part, a “tipping point” would be reached at which the police would be overwhelmed and the government forced to negotiate. As such he was quickly established as the figurehead, if not the actual head, of an organisation that was putatively decentralised.
More than anything else, though, it was the quasi-messianic role that Hallam played within the movement that intrigued me. A tall man, he has the severe countenance of all those furrow-faced elders that glare from the darkness of Caravaggio’s paintings. Where he goes, a trail of rapt activists often follows. When he speaks, his style is that of the prophet, in one breath presenting himself as a “meek analyst” and in the next foretelling of a weather-ravaged future in which marauding gangs will pillage your home and rape your sister. At the Cambridge Union last year, I watched him puncture the clubbable atmosphere of the debating chamber by telling 300 or so students, “Your generation is f***ed. Just accept it,” before rounding off the speech with the proposition, “I put it to you tonight that you are engaged in a project to kill millions and millions of people.”
For the most part, this mode of oration falls on stony ground. (That night in Cambridge, Hallam and his debating partner, Rupert Read, another XR leader, were accused by audience members of alienating the room with their “patronising” tone.) But for a small contingent of listeners, it has the power to imbue lasting devotion. In reporting on Hallam’s groups, I have shimmied down the verges of motorways and overnighted on Whitehall with priests, head teachers and GPs, all of whom heard his call to action, risked arrest and imprisonment, and put their faith in his ideology of change. And so when I ask him whether he had a religious upbringing, I don’t find it very surprising when the answer is, “Yes, very.”
He grew up in Hazel Grove, a suburb of Stockport on the outer edge of Manchester, where his mother was a minister with the local Methodist church. “If you know anything about northern Methodism, it’s 90 per cent morality and 10 per cent God,” he tells me. The household was a strict and traditional one. The child who would one day lead the radical flank of British environmentalism was taught “moderation in all things” by his parents. “I don’t really know why I ended up being and feeling different from other people. But there is a northern liberal morality that is very moderate and conservative in many ways, particularly in terms of personal morality. But in terms of social morality, it’s extremely clear that you should enter the public sphere if you see wrongdoing happening.”
His mother and father, who was a manager at a factory, were both members of the Liberal Party and would spend their weekends leafleting. Aged 14, Hallam read up on nuclear war (“It took me two f***ing years to recover from that”) and started going on marches with the peace movement. When he was 18 he went to India with the Methodists as part of the Student Christian Movement to work with civil rights groups in Raipur. When he came back, he took up a place at the London School of Economics but dropped out after a year to become a full-time campaigner. In 1986 he established Radical Routes, a network of workers’ co-operatives.
But then the Nineties came along and all of a sudden there was no Cold War and no Margaret Thatcher to organise against. “The culture coming in was very much every person for themselves,” he recalls. “I felt like a fish out of water and I just thought, if that’s the way society is and wants to be, it’s not for me to tell people what to do.” And so, aged 29, with his partner and two young children, he moved to Carmarthenshire in Wales to run an organic vegetable farm. “I thought that was it. Roger Hallam did a bit of radicalness in his early twenties, did some social economy type stuff and, like 99.9 per cent of the population, just got drawn into that neoliberal comfort zone.”
It is at this point that the biography starts to bend towards the arc of origin myth. In June 2007 it started raining and it didn’t stop for seven weeks, he says. The same thing happened the following year, by which point he was ruined. He laid off 20 employees and spent the next five years farming in a polytunnel trying to get himself out of a £100,000 hole of debt. “To see all those vegetables die was… I hesitate to say traumatising, because I don’t want to imply I’m some sort of snowflake. But it was enormously upsetting. And that’s when I said, well, I’ve got a skill set. I’m a good campaigner. I’m a good organiser. There’s no point me sitting around in Wales being miserable, weeding carrots.”
In 2015, he moved back to London to begin a PhD studying the methods of Martin Luther King and Mahatma Gandhi at KCL and three years later started XR. Within two months of the April 2019 rebellion the government had been forced into both declaring a climate emergency and legislating for net zero, with other governments around the world soon to follow suit. XR did not achieve all its three aims — Britain has a net zero target for 2050 as opposed to the demanded 2025. But to consider that only four years previously Hallam had been squelching around west Wales, struggling to earn a living, it was a remarkably rapid achievement.
SOMETIME AROUND THIS STAGE the café begins to close. By now, the photographer, Jamie’s, arms have given way and he has mounted the camera on a pile of books. Hallam, though, who has not touched the glass of tap water he opted for instead of my offer of a coffee, shows no sign of tiring. The café owners say they will stay open for us and we press on as the lights switch off around us. “Indefatigable” is one of the descriptors that comes up repeatedly when I ask people within XR what it’s like to work with Hallam. Alanna Byrne, who worked on XR’s media team, says the first time she met him was in 2016 at a squat in Haggerston, east London, after seeing a flyer advertising a talk on revolution. She and her friend were the only two to turn up after Hallam put the wrong date on the poster. He spoke for three hours regardless. “I was completely blown away by him,” Byrne remembers. “His drive is one in a million.”
Another word that comes up is “stubborn”. In Rebellion, a documentary about XR released last year, the impression is of a man blinkered to the point of unfeeling by his own dogma of social change. A few months after the success of April 2019, a rift develops between him and other leaders of the movement, not least his daughter Savannah, whom we see telling her father “f*** you” as she storms out of a strategy meeting. Hallam had wanted to fly a drone near Heathrow airport. Others did not think this a good idea, instead arguing for the need to build their position through political dialogue. “My view is that if you’re not in prison, you’re not in resistance,” he broods in the film. Others did not agree. After being arrested with a drone outside the airport and remanded in jail, Hallam was later voted off XR’s top table, effectively jettisoning him from the group.
And so having come in from the cold, Hallam is once again on the outside. As XR has become more moderate — earlier this year declaring in a statement entitled “We quit” that it would be shifting away from public disruption — Hallam’s theory of change has become more radical. Getting arrested for smashing the windows of a bank or spraying paint over a public building is no longer enough. It is mass imprisonment that he now believes will force the government to act. That was the thinking behind Insulate Britain, a group of roughly 100 hardliners. Gone are the days when he had the run of the XR offices in London. Now he strategises in the spare bedroom of his flat, which he funds through raising £2,000 worth of donations each month. When I ask him how he felt about being removed from XR he reflects for a moment, and I wonder if perhaps this might provoke a display of emotion. But, ever the analyst, he says, “I think that it’s been healthy, that there’s a number of different campaigns now.” He is unfazed too about the diminishing returns of his civil disobedience model, which since 2019 has failed to notch up any major wins while sending dozens of people to prison. He compares it to Black Lives Matter, which, though founded in 2013, only became a mass movement in 2020 after the murder of George Floyd. “At some point there’s going to be a major catastrophe… and then you’re going to have millions of people out on the street and you’ll have thousands of people getting arrested. The jails will be filling up and it’ll be a big shit show.”
This is the point at which journalists will be locked up and politicians will be lynched, the point otherwise known as revolution, which he thinks has been an inevitability since the mid-2010s when “the liberal class failed to get their act together on the climate”. “It’s not pretty,” he says of this future hellscape, which he believes could be reality within the next decade, by which time he says that one billion people will be living in parts of the globe made uninhabitable by global warming. When I tell him that the World Bank puts this figure at just over a fifth of what he states, and by the 2050s not 2030s, he seems unconcerned by the discrepancy. “Who cares, right, at the end of the day?” he says.
I understand the point he is making — that the prognosis is dire either way — but I don’t agree with it. For the change to happen, people need to believe that there is something worth acting for. In Hallam’s world, where carnage lies in wait whatever the action taken, that hope is non-existent. “He has apocalyptic images in his head and he shares them,” Gail Bradbrook, who remains part of XR, tells me. “I think that’s not always the best way to mobilise people — with fear. I think it needs balancing with spirit and vision for where humanity can go and I think XR was at its strongest when there was a balance between the light and the darkness.”
By the same token, XR’s retreat from disruption is an acknowledgment of the need to bring people with you, including politicians. The science is clear that governments around the world are not doing enough to forestall the catastrophic effects of global warming. But by and large, people don’t want, and can’t afford, to get arrested, even if their lives or their children’s lives depend on it.
Putting all this to him, he refers me once more to “the literature”, which I am informed supports his position. And I suspect it makes little difference to him at all that he is now at odds not only with most of society but with the climate movement more widely – for that is how, in the books, it is written.
“Martin Luther King was the most unpopular man in America in 1961. They all thought he was a communist and 70 per cent of the American public disagreed with the civil rights campaigns — similar to Insulate Britain. And then, of course, by 1968 he is, as you know, a saint.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Quentin Letts: MPs think Met chief Rowley is talking through his hat
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Make way, please, for the police commissioner’s hat. The home affairs committee was about to interview, under caution, Sir Mark Rowley, head of the Metropolitan Police. Rowley, who could be a younger brother of the late TV presenter Jim Bowen, was in uniform shirt with large epaulettes. And here came his cap. As at ancient Delphi, where priestesses carried temple wreaths, Rowley’s cap was borne by a female attendant of stately tread. And what a cap it was, the peak made of gleaming black plastic decorated by silver oak leaves. The cap was given a chair of its own.
The day began with the government meeting its target of hiring an additional 20,000 police officers. Given that many Tories think the police are useless wokies, you may wonder why they want another 20,000 of them. Yvette Cooper, shadow home secretary, was appalled by the recruiting success. She called it “a joke”. Yvette does not do jokes.
The committee was less interested in hiring new police than in firing the old ones, hundreds having records of sexual misbehaviour. “We’re sacking them at twice the previous rate,” boasted Rowley. Yet now there are 20,000 more police. It calls to mind the old story about the petrol pump attendant who, while filling a Rolls-Royce, begged the owner to switch off its engine, explaining: “She’s gaining on me, sir.”
Lee Anderson (C, Ashfield) was soon making life pitchy for Rowley, telling him to vacate his “ivory tower” and “sort out” the eco-campaigners who have turned parts of Westminster into a middle-class hippy campsite. Road traffic has been blocked. Anderson said taxi and bus drivers were fed up. Why were the protesters not being arrested for obstructing the highway? Rowley claimed that the law would not permit that. Committee members: “That’s not right.” Rowley to Anderson: “You’re making selective comments based on a partial understanding of the law.” (Translation: “You’re thick.”) Anderson: “I feel I’m wasting my time with you, to be honest.” Rowley: “If you want to be personally offensive, then write it in newspapers. I’m not going to answer these questions.” Dame Diana Johnson (Lab, Hull North) hoped no one was trying to be offensive — then took the mickey out of Rowley for the way the police trotted and cycled alongside Rishi Sunak’s car the other day. “Some of them looked a bit out of puff,” laughed Johnson.
Tim Loughton (C, East Worthing) told Rowley that when ten “rather shabby eco-terrorists” paralysed central London and the police did naff all, it was no surprise the public were giving up on the Met. Rowley: “We have to allow some obstruction of the highway.” The committee thought he was talking through his hat.
Talking of which, I followed him down the corridor afterwards. The cap was still in the hands of its reverent bearer. Rowley also had two bodyguards, presumably to protect him from Tory MPs rather than from Just Stop Oil protesters.
PMQs in the Commons being little more than an exchange of election slogans, greater sport was to be had at a Lords committee where retired mandarins were deploring, with delicious distaste, the recent “defenestration” of Whitehall permanent secretaries. Barbarians were at the gates, “good manners” were being ruptured and “civil service impartiality” — a concept that sign-language interpreters convey by laughing and spanking their thighs — was imperilled.
Lord Sedwill, former cabinet secretary, claimed to have no idea of the political leanings of Lord Macpherson, former Treasury supremo; Lord Macpherson claimed to have no idea of the voting habits of Sir Tom Scholar, who was catapulted out of the Treasury last autumn. And how horribly quick poor Tom’s sacking had been! Lord Mancroft (C), without quite saying “aw diddums”, pointed out that in the private sector sackings were invariably swift. Such was life. Sedwill, with a shudder: “One has to be careful about private and public sector analogies.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.title: Just Stop Oil protesters disrupt London traffic with slow marches
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.subtitle: Group describes jailed climate activists as ‘political prisoners’
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.text:
Just Stop Oil activists slowed traffic in parts of London down to a crawl with their latest series of “slow marches”.
More than 160 climate activists unveiled orange banners at seven locations in the West End, Westminster and south London before forming a line and slowly walking down the roads from 7am. The affected areas include Haymarket, a major thoroughfare that runs between Picadilly Circus and Pall Mall.
Just Stop Oil, which campaigns to end the use of fossil fuels in the UK through direct action, said the march was “in solidarity with the UK’s political prisoners”, including those “wrongly imprisoned for resisting the government’s genocidal plans to license over 100 new oil and gas projects by 2025”.
The protest comes days after Morgan Trowland, 40, and Marcus Decker, 34, were jailed for causing a public nuisance after they scaled the Dartford Crossing and brought gridlock to the area for two days as police closed the bridge to traffic. Trowland was sentenced to three years in prison while Decker was sentenced to two years and seven months.
Pia Bastide, 29, a full-time volunteer with the protest group who took part in the slow marches, said: “I feel that civil resistance is my moral duty. I was brought up to know the difference between right and wrong — and what this murderous, corrupted government is doing is plain wrong.
“Putting my freedom on the line is the least I can do to ensure my loved ones and I have a liveable future. We need to stand up to a government that does not have our best interests at heart and that is determined to sell our futures, one new oil licence at a time.”
Marcin Wawrzyn, 42, a construction worker from London taking part in the demonstration, said: “I work in construction and I am here because the British government is messing with laws of physics. New oil and gas is genocide and they know it. I was ten years old when I first heard of climate change. That was 30 years ago. I won’t be sitting around and waiting for another three decades.
“I’m back to work in two weeks’ time and I will get stuck in this traffic myself. And it’s worth it. And I would tell these people this is bigger than World War Two, the miners’ strike and the Berlin Wall, bigger than the poll tax riots. We need a human tipping point. It’s time to pick a side. We can win this.”
Supporters later planned to join Extinction Rebellion in a march from Parliament Square to the Shell Centre, the global headquarters of the oil company. Just Stop Oil has also warned of planned marches “every Saturday” at Parliament Square “until we win”.
Since the campaign group launched in April last year there have been more than 2,100 arrests.
A Metropolitan Police spokesman said: “Protesters from Just Stop Oil are causing disruption to roads in the Haymarket area of central London. Officers are on scene and we’ll aim to get traffic moving again freely as soon as it is safe to do so.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/king-ch.title: King Charles, the environmentalist — from ‘dotty’ to green prophet
https://www.thetimes.com/article/king-ch.text:
“This is a call to revolution. The Earth is under threat. It cannot cope with all that we demand of it. It is losing its balance and we humans are causing this to happen.”
Although they may sound like it, these are not the words of an Extinction Rebellion activist bellowing from the barricades. Nor are they those of Greta Thunberg lacerating chief executives at Davos. Rather, they’re the words of the new occupant of that renowned den of revolutionary fervour — Buckingham Palace.
Perhaps the most remarkable thing about these words, which begin the 2010 book Harmony: A New Way of Looking at Our World, by Charles, then Prince of Wales, is how unsurprising it is that he should have written them. Their grief-stricken urgency is entirely in keeping with the way he has been talking about the environment for half a century. All his adult life he has been calling for what he terms a “sustainability revolution” in how we view, value and make use of the natural world.
His environmentalism has been the thread connecting so many of his endeavours, from the Prince’s Rainforests Project, established in 2007 to combat deforestation, to his organic food range Duchy Originals, to the reed beds that filter sewage from Highgrove House, his 18th-century estate.
He has been mocked for it — including on Spitting Image, when his latex puppet invited a potted plant to his 40th birthday party. And he has been fêted for it, his friend Tony Juniper, the chairman of Natural England, having called him “possibly the most significant environmentalist in history”.
We have grown used to him banging on about it. As such, it’s easy to overlook just how curious it is that the House of Windsor — perhaps the most conservative institution on the planet — now has a figurehead who thinks we need to change our entire economic model or face ecological catastrophe. That these days many other people think it too makes it hard to appreciate just how unusual Charles’s environmentalism once was.
Speaking in 2020, he recalled that, when he first started addressing the subject in public, people thought him “rather dotty”. He delivered his first speech about it in 1970, at the age of 21, at the countryside steering committee for Wales. It was a jeremiad that could be repeated, almost word for word, at an environmental conference today.
“There are 55 million of us on this island using nonreturnable bottles and indestructible plastic containers,” he said. “It is not difficult to imagine the mountains of refuse that we shall have to deal with somehow.
“There is the growing menace of oil pollution at sea, which almost destroys beaches and certainly destroys tens of thousands of seabirds. There is chemical pollution discharged into rivers from factories and chemical plants, which clogs up the rivers with toxic substances and adds to the filth in the seas. There is air pollution from smoke and fumes discharged by factories and from gases pumped out by endless cars and aeroplanes.”
Unlike the change-hungry green activists coming of age today, the young Charles’s environmental anxieties sprang from his sense that society was simply changing too fast. “By the 1960s the industrialised countries were well on the way to creating what many imagined would be a limitless age of convenience,” he wrote in Harmony. “Even as a teenager I felt deeply disturbed by what seemed to have become a dangerously short-sighted approach.”
His thinking took a more mystical turn in the late Seventies, when his friend Robin Sheepshanks introduced him to Laurens van der Post, a South African explorer, writer and serial self-mythologiser, who became his spiritual guru, appealing to the young man’s desire for a sense of mission.
Van der Post believed that, through the medium of the natural world, ancient societies had felt an intuitive connection to the divine, but that modern society’s obsession with scientific rationality had severed this link. He encouraged Charles to believe that he could heal this rift, writing to him that “the battle for our renewal can be most naturally led by what is still one of the few great living symbols accessible to us — the symbol of the crown”.
At van der Post’s prompting, Charles developed a belief system he called “whole-ism”. The basis of whole-ism is Charles’s appreciation of nature as more than the sum of its parts — a harmonious order that emerges spontaneously from the interplay of millions of species.
He believes that God created that order, that we can see his genius in its workings, and that the way for us to live good, happy lives is to accept the constraints of our place within it. In that sense, as Charles sees it, building a sustainable economy isn’t just about staving off environmental disaster, it’s about restoring humanity’s proper relationship with the divine.
“Our intuition is deeply rooted in the natural order,” he wrote in Harmony. “If we were to recognise this, we would perhaps once again begin to see our existence in its proper place within creation.”
His belief that it is ungodly to tamper with nature has led him to some of the stances for which many people think him a bit kooky — like his opposition to genetically modified crops. It’s also the root of his dislike of modernist architecture, which he thinks makes people unhappy because its rectilinear shapes aren’t found in nature.
Although that may all sound a little esoteric, there is also a much more hard-headed, practical side to Charles’s environmentalism. He is keenly aware that the particular gift he can offer to the environmental movement is his ability to gather many important people in one room.
“He’s the world’s best convenor by a golden mile,” said his friend Patrick Holden, the former head of the Soil Association, a food and farming charity. “No one has more convening power, and I suspect no one ever will.”
“When you are in his attention field, which might only be for a few minutes, when he’s working a room of a hundred people, for some reason that is hard to define you feel that he gets you. He’ll say something to you that might only be short but is entirely relevant. Not many people can do that.”
In 1991, a year before the Rio Earth Summit that kicked off the international effort to limit climate change, the prince held a reception for delegates aboard the Royal Yacht Britannia, anchored off the coast of Brazil. The Brazilian president Fernando Collor de Mello was among the guests, as was William K Reilly, the head of the US Environmental Protection Agency.
The most impressive recent display of his convening power is the Sustainable Markets Initiative, which he launched at the World Economic Forum annual meeting in Davos in 2020. The initiative is a forum, open to companies that have committed to the goals of net zero and nature restoration, in which they can share knowledge about how to do so. Its nearly 500 members include Accenture, Aviva and Hewlett Packard Enterprise.
“When you get people round a table, you discover that frequently it’s the first time they’ve all sat round a table,” Charles told his biographer Catherine Mayer. “You think, this can’t be possible. They must have sat and talked. These are people you’d think would form a sensible, integrated approach. Not a bit of it.”
By his own admission Charles was once an “inveterate interferer and meddler”, dispatching memos to politicians on subjects ranging from alternative herbal medicines to bovine tuberculosis. Now he is king he will have to be much more circumspect. He has already shown that he understands that, having followed the government’s advice not to attend Cop27 in Egypt in November despite desperately wanting to go. At Cop26 in Glasgow the previous year he gave a set-piece speech, calling for “a vast military-style campaign to marshal the strength of the global private sector” to fix the climate crisis.
The change in Charles’s manner since he became king is obvious to Holden, who has recently attended two meetings at Buckingham Palace. “He doesn’t speak. He can no longer speak. And yet the room was full of prime ministers, NGO people like me and business leaders, and they all come because they respect him so deeply. He works the room, but it’s much more subtle.”
“He’s an enormous inspiration,” Juniper adds. “I think it’s wonderful that we have someone who’s now sovereign who has that history of interest in subjects that really are the most important for humankind as we go into the 21st century. I think we should all be extremely pleased that we have someone with that insight and that track record.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/camilla.subtitle: The Duke of Sussex described his stepmother as ‘dangerous’ in his autobiography and accused her of playing a ‘long game’ to marry the future King
https://www.thetimes.com/article/camilla.text:
The Queen’s son has rebutted Prince Harry’s claims that she played “the long game” and courted the King as part of a “campaign aimed at marriage . . . and the crown”.
Tom Parker Bowles insisted his mother Camilla had no “end game” in mind and married Charles purely for love.
Speaking on The News Agents podcast, he said: “I think change happens but I don’t care what anyone says — this wasn’t any sort of end game. She married the person she loved and this is what happened.”
• Prince Harry’s next encounter with ‘steely’ Camilla should terrify him
His remarks counter allegations by his stepbrother, the Duke of Sussex, who branded Camilla “dangerous” in his autobiography Spare. Prince Harry wrote how she had played “the long game”, with a campaign to secure marriage and ultimately “the crown”.
In interviews to promote his book, Harry referred to Camilla as a “villain” and spoke of bodies being “left in the street” during efforts to rehabilitate her image. He described in his memoir how he and his brother William, now the Prince of Wales, pleaded with their father not to wed Camilla, saying: “He didn’t answer. But she answered. Straight away. Shortly after our private summits with her, she began to play the long game. A campaign aimed at marriage, and eventually the crown, with Pa’s blessing we presumed.”
• King Charles’s coronation: everything we know so far
On the podcast, Parker Bowles, who is a food writer and food critic, would not be drawn into a discussion about whether there was panic over the possibility of Harry and his wife Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, not attending the coronation. Harry is now attending on his own. He told Emily Maitlis and Jon Sopel, the show’s hosts: “Nothing to do with me at all, though I did ask if Harry Kane was going as captain of England . . . My mother didn’t know . . . I don’t know if he’s coming.”
Asked if his mother will be anxious ahead of the coronation on May 6, he said it is “tough” to take on such a role during the ceremony but “she’s never complained”. “I think anyone would be anxious on an occasion of this sort of importance in terms of the historical. . . And yes, I think I’d be terrified if I had to sort of walk out wearing ancient robes . . . ” he said. “She’s 75, but you know, it’s tough to do it. But she’s never complained. You just do it. Get on with it.”
Parker Bowles praised the new King and Queen, saying: “I think they’re doing amazingly. I think King Charles is a good, kind, intelligent man who cares deeply about his roles wherever they may be, Prince of Wales, the King,” he said.
• Who will attend King Charles’s coronation? The expected guest list
He also championed Charles for being “way ahead of his time” on issues such as sustainability, food security, farming and pollution. “People were calling him sort of mad and eccentric 20 years ago. Everything that he’s talked about are now things that have hit the mainstream and now we’re really worrying about,” he said.
• How to watch the King’s coronation: TV channels and timings
Asked if it is strange to think of his mother as “the Queen”, Parker Bowles added: “Not really because she’s still our mother. I say ‘our’ but not the royal ‘we’, speaking for my sister and me. She’s our mother.” He disclosed that he will not be getting a title, adding: “You’re not going to find us with great estates and being called the duke of whatever. No. That would be appalling.”
Parker Bowles also supported the right to protest when asked if he was worried about demonstrations by Republic, the anti-monarchy group. The Times revealed this week that more 1,350 people have pledged to protest along the coronation parade route next month, and plan to boo loudly and chant “Not my King” when Charles passes them.
“Everyone has the right to think what they want . . . Going back to Extinction Rebellion and Animal Rebellion and Republic whatever it is, everyone has a right to their say,” he said. “We live in, thankfully, a free country . . . If people want to protest that’s their right to do so . . . ”
Republic is set to stage its largest protest action so far by lining the coronation procession route and gathering in Trafalgar Square on the day of the ceremony.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.title: Just Stop Oil pair jailed over Dartford Crossing protest
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.text:
Just Stop Oil (JSO) protesters who scaled the Dartford Crossing and brought gridlock to the bridge for two days have been jailed for up to three years.
Morgan Trowland, 40, and Marcus Decker, 34, used ropes and other climbing equipment to scale the 84m Queen Elizabeth II Bridge, which links the M25 in Essex and Kent.
The bridge was closed from 4am on October 17 last year to 9pm the following day, with jams as traffic was forced to use the tunnels instead.
Both defendants were found guilty on Friday by unanimous verdicts of causing a public nuisance, following an earlier trial.
Judge Shane Collery KC sentenced Trowland at Southend crown court to three years in prison, while Decker was jailed for two years and seven months.
“You have to be punished for the chaos you caused and to deter others from copying you,” he said.
The judge said that Trowland, who has six previous convictions relating to protests, had a “leading role”, while Decker had one previous conviction relating to a protest.
The judge said that the pair “plainly believed you knew better than everyone else”, adding: “In short, to hell with everyone else.
“By your actions you caused this very important road to be closed for 40 hours,” the judge said, noting that the disruption affected “many tens of thousands, some very significantly”.
It comes as a split within JSO has emerged over whether it will protest at the London Marathon on Sunday.
• Just Stop Oil bankrolled by fossil fuel heiress whose cash pays activists to protest
A JSO activist, Phoebe Plummer, one of the protesters who threw tomato soup at Vincent van Gogh’s Sunflowers, told TalkTV that it would not cause chaos at the race.
However, the official Twitter account for JSO posted a message under a recording of Plummer’s interview saying: “I think Phoebe missed the meeting last night.”
Extinction Rebellion, which is organising what could be the largest climate change protest in years, has said that it will not disrupt the marathon, having recently vowed to de-escalate its tactics, and has even said it will help to guard the event.
The Times can also reveal that JSO is spending almost £1 million a year carrying out its campaign of civil disobedience.
Roger Hallam, the founder of Extinction Rebellion and now a co-ordinator for JSO, told a meeting earlier this month that the group is spending £80,000 a month on its activities.
The former organic farmer, who was released from prison earlier this year after being held in relation to protests on the M25, added that regular monthly donations to the group stand at £20,000.
It has also received additional money from high-profile donors such as the Hollywood director Adam McKay, football club owner Dale Vince and the Los Angeles-based Climate Emergency Fund, linked to the oil heiress Aileen Getty.
In a recording of the meeting heard by The Times, Hallam said it has been providing financial support to 100 of its most devoted activists, spending money providing safe houses, transport and basic expenses.
He said that one unnamed individual pledged £200,000 after the recent fundraising meeting in Britain.

Marcus Decker was jailed for two years and seven months

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/floo.title: Floored by Kipchoge (the dog), but is Emile Cairess the heir to Farah?
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/floo.subtitle: The 25-year-old from Yorkshire, making his London Marathon debut on Sunday, has been tipped to make a big impression
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/floo.text:
With Sir Mo Farah confirming that Sunday’s London Marathon will be his final race at the distance, eyes will begin to turn to the future.
Enter Emile Cairess. The 25-year-old is making his marathon debut this weekend, and hopes are high that he can make an instant impact.
Cairess has made a name for himself over the past year, most notably breaking the European ten-mile record in March. Finishing in 45min 57sec, Cairess beat the long-standing record of 46:02 set by Richard Nerurkar in 1993.
He is no stranger to racing on the big stage. He earned his first British vest in 2017, finishing eighth in the European Cross Country Championships, despite taking a tumble in the first kilometre. He won a bronze medal in the 10,000m at the European Under-23 Championships in 2019 and qualified for the 10,000m final at the senior 2022 European Championships.
Growing up in Yorkshire, Cairess first took to running at the age of five and would accompany his mum regularly on her three to four-mile runs.
His training partner, Phil Sesemann, partially inspired Cairess’s move up to the marathon distance, as the 30-year-old was the first Briton home on his debut in London two years ago. It gave Cairess the belief that he could do the same.
Cairess rarely accompanies Sesemann on long runs on a Sunday these days. Instead Kipchoge and Haile, two dogs named after legendary distance runners and owned by Sesemann, tag along — or at least they used to. One routine training run last year ended with Cairess on the floor after the dogs bundled him over. As a result of the incident, he now refuses to run with them.
Back to Sunday’s race, and Cairess isn’t short of quiet confidence. “Like any race, I want to perform my best and achieve a target, but I think the primary objective is to learn the race and have a good experience,” he said.
“Hopefully, I can take that to future races where I can be more competitive with the top guys, so this is just a platform for that.”
Despite his inexperience over the distance, there is a lot of buzz over Cairess’s potential in the marathon. The former British champion, Chris Thompson, likes his attitude.
“It’s refreshing to hear a young person be so positive,” Thompson said. “Emile has this presence about him that’s really impressed me, and I hope he keeps that because it’s not often that you get an athlete that’s precocious but humble and ambitious.”
There have been suggestions that Sunday’s race could be a target for protesters, after last weekend’s Grand National was delayed by animal rights activists, while a Just Stop Oil protest delayed a match at the World Snooker Championship on Monday. Cairess hopes there is no disruption.
“It’s an event that benefits a lot of people throughout the country. And I think for that to be interrupted would be a real shame,” Cairess said.
“It’s a good cause. Everyone’s concerned about the environment, and I think the majority of the people in the race will be concerned about the environment.”
The depth in British marathon running is improving all the time. Along with Cairess, 20 other Britons made the entry list for the men’s race — all of whom possess a personal best under 2hr 20min.
“Ten years ago you could qualify for the Olympics with a 2:13. You need to be five minutes faster now,” Cairess added. “That’s really given me and everyone else a kick up the backside.”
As Farah exits stage left and with the Olympic Games only 15 months away, the London Marathon could be the perfect place for Cairess to announce himself as the next big thing.
Dewi GriffithsAge: 31Marathon best: 2:09:49 (2017)The second-fastest Briton on paper, but the Welshman has recently struggled to replicate his best form, having been hit by injuries.
Chris ThompsonAge: 42Marathon best: 2:10:52 (2021)He may be the elder statesman of the field on Sunday, but Thompson still has the potential to produce a big performance. He qualified for his second Olympics in 2021, nine years after his first, and was the only Briton to finish the marathon in Tokyo, coming 39th.
Ben ConnorAge: 30Marathon best: 2:11:20 (2020)The Derby-based athlete enjoyed an impressive marathon debut in London in 2020, before finishing second behind Thompson at the Olympic trials in 2021. However, he struggled in the heat in Tokyo and failed to finish.
Luke CaldwellAge: 31Marathon best: 2:11:33 (2022)Impressed on his marathon debut in Houston last year, clocking his best time to date, and was rewarded with a place in the 2022 European Championship marathon, but failed to finish. This will be his first attempt at the London Marathon.
Weynay GhebresilasieAge: 29Marathon best: 2:11:57 (2022)
The British champion competed for Eritrea in the steeplechase at the London 2012 Olympics, before seeking asylum and settling in the UK. Set a personal best in last year’s London Marathon.
Phil SesemannAge: 30Marathon best: 2:12:10 (2022)The Leeds-based athlete was the first Briton home in the 2021 London Marathon, running 2:12:58 on his distance debut. Should the junior doctor perform to his capabilities, he could be in line to break the 2:10 mark.
Ross BradenAge: 29Marathon best: 2:14:32 (2022)The Kent athlete was the third Briton home in last year’s London Marathon, behind Ghebresilasie and Sesemann. Has spent most of this year so far training in Kenya.
